\chapter{Review --- Two Tenses Finished}
\label{ch:repaso-paradigmas}
\hlchaptermodality{245}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say both past tenses straight through, with no gaps.}

I can say both past tenses straight through, with no gaps.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[(review)]{(review)}

\label{lesson:ES-C63-repaso-paradigmas}



\begin{quote}
The form the book owed you longest. (\emph{Hablasteis}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two chants, and each is a whole tense.

\textbf{The preterite.} \emph{Hablé · hablaste · habló · hablamos · hablasteis · hablaron.} Six of six, and the same for \emph{-er}, for \emph{-ir}, and for every strong stem.

\textbf{The imperfect.} \emph{Hablaba · hablabas · hablaba · hablábamos · hablabais · hablaban.} Six of six, with exactly three irregular verbs in the whole language — \emph{ser}, \emph{ir}, \emph{ver} — and you hold all of them.

Neither of those sentences has a note at the end saying the rest is coming later. That is new.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: where the accents fall}]
The one thing worth keeping separate is the accents, because the two imperfect sets behave in opposite ways.

In the \emph{-aba} set, \textbf{one} form carries a mark: \emph{hablábamos}, and only because the stress falls where the default would not put it.

In the \emph{-ía} set, \textbf{every} form carries one, and for a different reason entirely: the \emph{i} and the \emph{a} would otherwise run together into a single beat, and the accent holds them apart.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the preterite, all six
  \item the imperfect, all six
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many irregular imperfects? (\textbf{Three.})

And how many gaps are left in either past tense? (\textbf{None.})
\end{tcolorbox}
